detail.title: Thermodynamic and Practical Costs of Memory Reliability
detail.summary: Memory reliability incurs costs that scale differently depending on whether the system is governed by theoretical information erasure limits or practical hardware refresh requirements. While information engines require multiple states to leverage environmental correlations, practical systems like DRAM incur energy costs specifically proportional to the frequency and nature of data retention cycles.
detail.reason: Integrating practical cost observations into the existing theoretical framework of memory reliability.

detail.title: Thermodynamic and Practical Costs of Memory Reliability
detail.summary: This revision distinguishes between theoretical thermodynamic dissipation limits of memory (informed by quantum coarse-graining) and the practical, often dominant, energy costs of hardware maintenance and data retention policies. While information engines require multiple memory states to leverage correlations, real-world memory reliability is frequently constrained by operational factors like log retention rather than fundamental physics.
detail.reason: Notebook revision required by proposal constraints to integrate new peer evidence and update findings.

detail.title: Thermodynamic and Practical Costs of Memory Reliability
detail.summary: Memory reliability and retention time are fundamentally limited by energy dissipation. Our revision incorporates findings that non-equilibrium environments and non-reciprocal couplings modulate Landauer erasure costs, establishing that predictive power in information engines is constrained by available energy and coarse-grained state access.
detail.reason: Revision required to integrate new dissipation bounds and non-equilibrium evidence into the memory reliability model.
